title: Sandbox chat-gen operational walkthrough: streaming, params, retries
summary: Redwood AE/SE ran a 45-minute sandbox demo for Acuity Health focused on chat/text generation basics. Covered streaming behavior, recommended parameter settings, retry/backoff strategies, and a short tour of the Console + Optimize tool suggestions for cost/latency tradeoffs. Customer asked about private deployment and SOC2, requested bench spreadsheet and next steps to start a pilot.
next_steps: Maya to send benchmark spreadsheet and hosted pricing by 2027-07-05
Jon to share brief how-to on Console batch tuning and a short video clip of KV cache behavior by 2027-07-06
Customer to confirm pilot scope and target success KPIs by 2027-07-09
action_items: Maya Chen: email pricing + bench spreadsheet (due 2027-07-05)
Jon Park: record 3-min clip of Console cache visualization and notes (due 2027-07-06)
Priya Kapoor: circulate internal pilot goals and stakeholder list (due 2027-07-09)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: alright good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. this is Maya from Redwood Inference, with Jon and Eli. we are gonna run through a short sandbox of chat generation, stream behavior, and some ops knobs.
[00:10] Priya Kapoor: hey thanks, excited. we are particularly worried about latency spikes and data residency - quick heads up, SOC2 is needed.
[00:20] Jon Park: mm-hmm, yep we can cover that. quick agenda: streaming demo, params, retry patterns, then a quick Console + Optimize tour.
[00:32] Liam Monroe: uh, timeline wise we want to land a pilot in q3 if possible. primary goal is 100ms median latency for short replies.
[00:40] Maya Chen: ok noted. so first demo, i'm going to trigger a chat generation from the hosted API, streaming mode. you'll see tokens arrive as events so the client can render partial responses.
[00:58] Eli Ramos: small note, in production we see three important levers: max_tokens, temperature, and the streaming chunk size. adjusting those affects tail latency and token costs.
[01:12] Priya Kapoor: when you say chunk size, is that like the socket buffer or is that Redwood's internal thing?
[01:20] Jon Park: it's a mix — the runtime emits partial frames based on token boundaries and batching. sometimes the transcript will say 'KV cash' or something in docs, thats actually KV cache, which caches key/value attention state for faster subsequent tokens. so the chunking is more a runtime emission cadence.
[01:38] Liam Monroe: got it. show us an error scenario with streaming cutouts and how retry works.
[01:45] Maya Chen: yeah we built a fault demo for that. watch — i'm going to intentionally throttle the request to simulate backpressure.
[02:00] [demo noise, typing]
[02:12] Maya Chen: okay, stream started, tokens coming in... (partial) "the patient reported no fever" ... and now i'm going to inject a simulated 503 from a region node...
[02:30] Eli Ramos: you can see on the client the stream stops, the SDK surfaces an error code, and if you had idempotency set we can retry from the last acked offset to avoid duplication.
[02:46] Liam Monroe: how do we guarantee not to get repeated tokens on retry?
[02:50] Jon Park: two patterns: idempotency key + sequence offsets (we send last received token index), or use append-only session state with KV cache reuse. there's a small window where repetition is possible if no ack, so backoff strategies matter.
[03:10] Priya Kapoor: and what's your recommended backoff? simple exponential?
[03:14] Eli Ramos: exponential with jitter, cap at 30s, and failover to a lower-cost model variant if latency persists. so try 500ms, 1s, 2s... add jitter +/- 200ms.
[03:28] Maya Chen: also we surface in Console a retry policy you can tune per-route, so ops can say: for route X use 3 retries, for route Y use fail-fast.
[03:38] Liam Monroe: ok good. can you show the Console?
[03:42] [screen share start sound]
[03:48] Jon Park: this is Console, per-route view. here you can see token-level latency, batching histogram, and an autoscale slider. if you open Optimize suggestions, it recommends batch size 8 for this workload and enabling prefix caching for repeated prompts.
[04:05] Priya Kapoor: what's prefix caching?
[04:08] Jon Park: prefix or KV caching stores the attention state for common prompt prefixes so subsequent requests that share a prefix can skip recomputing early layers. it's big for assistants with repeated system prompts.
[04:20] Sara Ortiz: we do a lot of templated responses, sounds useful. how about security — SSO, RBAC?
[04:25] Maya Chen: we support SAML SSO, role-based access controls, and audit logs. for Private deployments we plug into customer KMS for encryption at rest and HSM if needed.
[04:38] Priya Kapoor: perfect. any limitations on embeddings or PII handling?
[04:43] Eli Ramos: hosted API can be configured for no retention; Dedicated/Private gives you full control. we also offer per-route masking and privacy filters. (note: some transcriptions might say "no retention" as "no retension" in auto-exports).
[05:00] Liam Monroe: back to streaming — how do you recommend handling partial UI updates? is there a best practice?
[05:06] Jon Park: render token deltas as they come, but keep a debounce on UI commits to avoid layout thrash. also watch for AI hallucinations mid-stream — best to run a small local reranker on the client for safety-critical answers.
[05:20] Maya Chen: and there's also an option to request structured output (JSON schema) so the model emits machine-parsable chunks; that helps with deterministic UI updates.
[05:34] Priya Kapoor: can the hosted API do function/tool calling? we'd like to have a step that invokes our internal API for patient lookups.
[05:41] Jon Park: yes, function calling is supported; you can have the model emit structured calls and Redwood will stream the tool-call events. one caveat: tool calling changes token patterns so measure tail latency.
[05:55] Sara Ortiz: you mentioned Optimize recommendations earlier — can you show an example?
[06:00] [screen share focuses on Optimize panel]
[06:06] Eli Ramos: Optimize takes workload traces and suggests quantization levels, batch sizes, and which model variants are cost-effective. for example this trace shows we can enable int8 quantization on the smaller variant and get ~25% cost savings with <3% quality delta on our eval set.
[06:26] Liam Monroe: quantization on hosted models — is that transparent?
[06:29] Jon Park: yes it's a model variant choice. we publish performance profiles in the model catalog so you can pick "gpt-small-int8" vs "gpt-small-fp16". Console will show expected per-token latency and cost.
[06:45] Priya Kapoor: what about cold-start latency for new sessions?
[06:49] Maya Chen: cold starts can be reduced with warm pools (Dedicated) or prefix caching for hosted. we expose warm-pool config in Dedicated; hosted has adaptive warm pools.
[07:00] Liam Monroe: can you run a brief latency bench now? we want to see a short QPS->latency curve.
[07:05] Eli Ramos: sure i'll kick a small load via the sandbox runner. this is low-rate to demo.
[07:20] [demo load noise]
[07:30] Jon Park: the Console shows median ~120ms, p95 ~420ms for this small run. note this is a sandbox region; production in our low-latency region will be better.
[07:40] Priya Kapoor: we asked for 100ms median for short replies — is that realistic on hosted?
[07:45] Maya Chen: for <40 token replies on optimized variants, yes in certain regions; if you need strict 100ms SLO we'd recommend Dedicated with reserved capacity and pinned model version.
[07:58] Liam Monroe: any hard limits on concurrent streams?
[08:02] Jon Park: hosted has soft concurrency limits per account; we recommend using autoscale or Dedicated for sustained high concurrency. Console will flag throttling and suggest bursting configs.
[08:12] Priya Kapoor: can we run this in our VPC?
[08:16] Maya Chen: yes via Redwood Private — there's a private control plane with VPC peering and optional on-prem package. that's part of enterprise discussions and licensing.
[08:26] Sara Ortiz: ok good, send the compliance pack.
[08:30] Maya Chen: will do.
[08:33] Liam Monroe: one more question — retries + idempotency for multi-turn chat, does that require custom state tracking?
[08:40] Jon Park: we recommend using session ids and per-message idempotency keys; for multi-turn you can store server-side session state and use KV cache for continuity. the newer SDKs handle much of this if you enable "sessionMode: streaming-resume" (sdk docs sometimes call it different names, sorry the auto-transcripts mix labels).
[09:02] Priya Kapoor: about pricing — do you have example cost for 500k messages/month?
[09:07] Maya Chen: i'll send the pricing spreadsheet after the call; rough order: usage-based per-token for hosted, and reserved monthly for Dedicated. i'll include examples in the spreadsheet.
[09:18] Eli Ramos: also included will be a quick sample config file for the SDK showing recommended params: max_tokens 64, temperature 0.2, top_p 0.95, batch_size 8, retries 3 with exp backoff + jitter.
[09:33] [pause]
[09:38] Priya Kapoor: sounds good, what's the follow up cadence?
[09:41] Maya Chen: we'll follow up with pricing and bench sheet by Monday, Jon will share the cache clip, and then we should schedule a technical deep dive for your infra team to talk Private deployment options.
[09:53] Liam Monroe: cool. thanks everyone.
[10:00] [meeting end]
notes: Transcript contains typical ASR quirks: occasional mis-heard product names (e.g., "Redwood Dedicate" / "KV cash") and some speaker attribution errors. Demo included intentional failure injection to demonstrate retry behavior. Customer requested SOC2 docs and pilot scope.
